title: Father's motives and the end of the family band
summary: His father, raised partly in an orphanage, gave the boys a family unit through music; the band faded as they got into jazz and high school.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Was your father, I’m not sure how to put this, was he living out a way of life that he wished he had had as a professional musician?

Could be. It’s very possible. Because you know he never had a childhood and he made sure that we had a real childhood and really had a family unit, which, you know, he was in an orphanage for a while so he made sure that we were in a good family unit and he told me that when he had three sons, you know that was a big deal having three sons, originally, because he did all kinds of carpentry and odd jobs. He figured he could have his own construction company with three boys, three sons, you could really do well. But he also gave us the music. So you know he didn’t have money so basically he gave us that opportunity. And you’ve got to remember, being a musician back then was not a real © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

job. No one thought you could make a living doing that. But he made sure that we had that foundation. Of course then when we went off on our own and started playing without the family band, you know, we were making money and gigging so I think he was kind of pleased about that. And I’m sure he would have loved to have been a professional out in the real world, out in the world, but he had so many bands in the area. He had marching bands, he had concert bands, dance bands, you name it. So he had bands for every occasion. When Mussolini’s brown shirts came to Mount Morris, he called ahead and found “Giovinezza” which was the theme song from Mussolini’s youth, the youth, Giovinezza, the youth. And when the brown shirts were marching down the street of Mount Morris he had the band start playing that and they were shocked and they gave the old salute to Mussolini. They were staying in Dansville at the McFadden mansion. He was a real right winger. I don’t know if you remember that.
I do — that’s the first I’ve heard about brown shirts anywhere in New York State.

Yeah, was it the brown shirts or the black shirts? I think it was the brown shirts. Whatever Mussolini’s youth group was. And this McFadden had a huge resort in Dansville, kind of a weird medical kind of a colon-cleansing and all that, he invited them to the United States before we got involved and all that. But Pop was always on top of things. He had that theme song. I’ve probably got it out in the garage. But no one even knew what that was.
What finally, everybody got older and was there a particular thing that caused the family band to go the way of all bands, eventually it has to end somewhere.

Well we were getting more into jazz and we were in high school, and we didn’t have the kind of time when we were in grade school to go out and gig all the time. Plus I think my parents were happy to have some time alone at home and get rid of the kids, get us out the door.
